# Zensus: Full Context for LLMs

> Cash flow forecasting and planning for businesses with unpredictable revenue.

## What Is Zensus?

Zensus is a financial planning tool that gives businesses of any size real-time visibility into their cash position and cash flow. Instead of spreadsheets or gut instinct, you connect your financial accounts and get instant, always-current projections, plus a cash flow agent you can ask questions in natural language.

## Problem It Solves

Most businesses make million-dollar decisions (hiring, fundraising timing, contract negotiations) based on gut feeling or a stale spreadsheet. Checking your bank balance is not a financial strategy. Zensus replaces that with live, subscription-aware projections that update automatically.

## Core Features

### Real-Time Cash Flow
- Calculates your exact zero-cash date based on connected financial data
- Bank data from Plaid and invoices and subscriptions from HubSpot update by webhook; QuickBooks syncs once a day
- Every source also refreshes when you open the app if its data is more than an hour old
- Manual sync available at any time

### Cash Flow Agent / Scenario Planning
- Ask natural-language questions: "Can I afford to hire two engineers?", "What if we lose our largest annual contract?", "What happens with 5% monthly churn?"
- Multi-turn conversations with persistent chat history

### Subscription-Intelligent Projections
- Syncs HubSpot subscriptions including annual and quarterly contracts
- Projects revenue based on when cash actually hits the bank, not flat monthly estimates
- Detects recurring income and expenses, including payroll, from your transaction history

- **Plaid**: Direct bank account connection for real-time transaction data
- **HubSpot**: Subscription and contract revenue sync

### Cash Flow Analysis
- Expense categorization across 8 business categories

- CSV export at monthly, weekly, or daily granularity
- Burn rate tracking and trend visualization

## FAQ

**Do I need QuickBooks to use Zensus?**
No. You can connect your bank account directly via Plaid, connect QuickBooks, sync your HubSpot subscriptions, or use any combination.

**Can I connect my HubSpot account?**
Yes. Zensus syncs your HubSpot subscriptions, including annual and quarterly contracts, so your cash flow projections reflect when revenue actually hits your bank.

**How long does setup take?**
A few minutes. Connect your bank or QuickBooks with one click, and your cash flow forecast is calculated instantly.

**What kind of questions can I ask?**
Anything about your finances: "When will I run out of cash?", "Can I afford to hire two engineers?", "What if we lose our largest annual contract?", "What happens with 5% monthly churn?"

**Is my financial data secure?**
Yes. Bank-level AES-256 encryption. Credentials are never stored; OAuth tokens are managed by Plaid and Intuit.

**Who can see my data?**
Only you. Your financial data is never shared, sold, or used to train AI models.

## Guides

### What Is Cash Flow Forecasting?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-is-cash-flow-forecasting

Cash flow forecasting estimates how much money a business will have available in the future by predicting when cash comes in and goes out. Key facts from the guide:

- Every forecast has four building blocks: opening cash, cash inflows, cash outflows, and closing cash, which becomes the next period's opening cash.
- Ending Cash = Opening Cash + Cash Inflows - Cash Outflows; $50,000 + $35,000 - $42,000 = $43,000.
- A month that ends at $21,000 can drop to $1,000 in Week 2, which is why weekly forecasts catch gaps monthly ones hide.
- The direct method suits short-term weekly forecasting; the indirect method suits longer-term planning. A 13-week direct-method rolling forecast is the recommended primary tool.
- A cash flow statement reports what happened, a forecast predicts what will happen, and a budget sets what you want to happen.

### What Is a 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-is-a-13-week-cash-flow-forecast

A 13-week cash flow forecast is a rolling, week-by-week projection of the cash you expect to receive and pay over the next 91 days. Key facts from the guide:

- It is a direct-method model built from real cash moving in and out, not derived from the P&L. Four lines: opening cash, cash inflows, cash outflows, closing cash.
- Closing Cash = Opening Cash + Cash Inflows - Cash Outflows; each week's closing balance becomes the next week's opening.
- Opening cash should be cash that is actually available to spend, and inflows should land when customers actually pay, not when the invoice is issued or the terms say.
- A month can end at $30,000 while week 2 closes at $7,000, $3,000 under a $10,000 floor; a monthly view hides that.
- In the worked 13-week example ($100,000 start, $40,000 floor), receipts total $320,000, payments $340,000, and week 13 closes at $80,000, but week 5 drops to $35,000, $5,000 below the floor.
- The forecast rolls: each week, compare forecast to actuals, ask why on big variances, drop the finished week, and add a new 13th week.
- A 13-week forecast is not a budget or a P&L: it is cash basis and rolling, where a budget and a P&L are accrual basis.
- ARR is not cash: a $30,000 annual prepayment is $30,000 of cash in month one but $2,500 a month of revenue on the P&L.
- For critical payments a daily view matters, because a healthy week-end balance can hide a midweek shortfall.
- A free downloadable 13-week template (XLSX with chained weekly balances and a cash buffer check) is available at https://zensus.finance/templates/13-week-cash-flow-template.xlsx, and a browser builder that fills in a first 13 weeks is at https://zensus.finance/tools/13-week-cash-flow-template

### Cash Flow Early Warning System
https://zensus.finance/blog/cash-flow-early-warning-system

How to detect a cash shortage before it happens: the indicators to watch, a minimum cash policy, and alerts that lead to action. Key facts from the guide:

- A cash flow early warning system combines reliable financial data, a forward-looking cash forecast, warning thresholds, and a process for acting when a threshold is crossed.
- Six warning signs: the lowest projected balance keeps falling, DSO rises (for example from 45 to 58 days), overdue receivables age faster (overdue concentration from 10% to 25%), one customer is a large share of expected collections (60% in the example), net burn rises, and the forecast keeps getting payment timing wrong.
- Cash headroom is the lowest projected balance minus the minimum cash threshold; an $18,000 low point against a $40,000 minimum is a $22,000 reserve shortfall.
- The zero-cash date is the first date projected cash reaches zero, found by dating every receipt and payment; a $50,000 customer payment moved four days later turns a week ending at $45,000 into a minus $5,000 Friday.
- A minimum cash policy adds the unavoidable outflows of a response window to a forecast error margin: $60,000 plus $9,000 gives a $69,000 minimum.
- The JPMorgan Chase Institute found a median of 27 cash buffer days across about 597,000 small businesses (September 2016); the 2026 AFP FP&A Benchmarking Survey found only 14% of finance teams formally track forecast accuracy.
- Zensus checks the 30-day cash projection after every sync and once a day, and posts a Slack alert when it drops below the cash floor you set.

### Predictive Cash Flow Forecasting
https://zensus.finance/blog/predictive-cash-flow-forecasting

How to see a cash shortfall before it happens by forecasting cash on the dates money actually arrives and leaves. Key facts from the guide:

- Revenue, profit, and cash measure different things; a profitable month can still contain a week where payroll is due before customer payments arrive.
- Forecast accuracy is measured against actuals: a forecast of $120,000 ending cash against an actual $105,000 is a 12.5% absolute percentage error, and the cause (late receivables, higher expenses, an earlier hire) decides the fix.
- Forecasting a range (optimistic, expected, pessimistic) shows the risk a single line hides; from $200,000, the three cases in the guide end three months later at $215,000, $155,000, and $50,000.
- Invoices should be dated by when the customer actually pays: a $40,000 invoice on 30-day terms from a customer who pays 15 days late arrives 45 days after it is issued.
- A week can end positive and still go negative in the middle: $35,000 opening cash, $28,000 payroll on Wednesday and a $12,000 vendor payment on Thursday reach minus $5,000 before a $30,000 payment lands on Friday.
- A one-hour starter forecast: 13 weeks by week, ending cash equals beginning cash plus cash received minus cash paid, then move the largest expected payment two weeks later and compare.
- Zensus projects cash by month, week, and day from Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot, and models a scenario (a hire, a lost customer, a one-off expense) against the baseline.

### Will I Make Payroll?
https://zensus.finance/blog/will-i-make-payroll

How to forecast payroll cash weeks ahead, by Zensus founder Ajin Sunny. Key facts from the guide:

- The question is not today's balance or payday: it is whether you have enough cleared, available cash on the date your payroll provider withdraws funds.
- Three dates differ: employee payday, the payroll funding date (when the provider withdraws), and the payroll submission deadline. Relay, for example, debits a set number of business days before payday, closer to payday for faster deposit speeds (1-day or 4-day direct deposit).
- A funding shortfall (balance below the provider withdrawal) means missing payroll; a reserve shortfall (cash left after payroll below your preferred floor) is a warning. Example: $42,000 available, a $28,000 withdrawal, $14,000 left, $1,000 under a $15,000 reserve, and payroll still clears.
- Available cash before payroll = starting usable cash + receipts that clear before the funding date - other payments. Funding gap = max(0, provider withdrawal - available cash). Reserve gap = max(0, preferred floor - after-payroll cash).
- Use the provider's total withdrawal (net pay plus withholdings and taxes it remits), not net pay, and date receipts by when they clear, not the invoice due date.
- Forecast at least two payroll cycles (about four weeks for biweekly pay); a rolling 13-week view shows when payroll, taxes and loan payments compete for the same week. Stress-test a late customer, an earlier funding date, and a commission spike.
- Gusto's 2026 research found about one-third of small businesses in its analysis had at least one payroll their balances did not cover; many bridged the gap with transfers, short-term financing or early invoice payments.
- Zensus detects payroll from recurring bank debits, projects cash to each payroll date, and sends a Slack alert when the 30-day projection drops below a user's floor.

### What Happens If You Miss Payroll?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-happens-if-you-miss-payroll

What a missed payroll sets off, and a seven-day plan for a founder who may not make the next one. The guide is not legal advice. Key facts from the guide:

- A seven-day recovery plan is not a seven-day legal grace period: employees are owed their wages on the required payday.
- Three situations get called "missing payroll": a missed provider submission deadline (employees may still be paid on time), a payroll debit the bank could not cover (employees may be paid late), and a missed payroll-tax deposit (employees are paid, the tax deposit is late).
- Worked example: a team of 12 with Wednesday payroll has $58,000 on Monday and $9,000 of rent on Tuesday, leaving $49,000 against $54,000 of wages and tax funding, a $5,000 gap; a $35,000 customer payment on Friday arrives too late.
- The FLSA requires wages due for a pay period to be paid on the regular payday, but its collection provisions mainly cover minimum wage and overtime; state law governs the rest.
- California Labor Code Section 210 sets $100 per employee for a first late-payment violation and $200 per employee plus 25% of the unpaid wages for later ones; Section 203 waiting-time penalties on final pay can reach 30 days of wages. Texas Workforce Commission guidance says it generally does not impose an administrative penalty for a first offense.
- Late payroll-tax deposits carry separate IRS penalties: 2% at 1 to 5 days, 5% at 6 to 15 days, 10% after 15 days, and 15% if unpaid more than 10 days after the first IRS notice or once an immediate-demand notice arrives, plus interest; the IRS can also pursue the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty against responsible individuals. Never divert payroll taxes to fund payroll.
- If full payroll cannot be funded, do not decide partial payments alone; talk to an employment lawyer.
- The seven-day plan: triage and tell employees (day 0), find the cash (1), fix what is due (2), build a daily 14-day forecast (3), find what went wrong (4), set a payroll buffer of one to two payroll runs (5), move to a 13-week rolling forecast (6), and fix the system with an owner, daily cash review, and an early warning below the buffer (7).

### Forecasting AI Compute Costs for Founders (2026)
https://zensus.finance/blog/forecasting-ai-compute-costs-for-founders

How to model AI inference and agent costs as a first-class line item in a cash flow forecast. Key facts from the guide:

- Goldman Sachs Research projects AI token consumption will multiply roughly 24 times by 2030, to about 120 quadrillion tokens a month.
- The inference cost paradox: per-token prices keep falling, yet total spend rises because usage grows faster than costs fall.
- Andreessen Horowitz observed in 2020 that AI companies often run gross margins in the 50% to 60% range, well below the 60% to 80% or more it gave as the benchmark for comparable SaaS businesses.
- A practical operator benchmark: keep inference spend below 10% of revenue for chat-heavy products. Zensus uses the same threshold in its own planning.
- Forecast AI compute under three scenarios (base, upside, downside) because usage-driven costs scale with adoption, not headcount.

### Runway vs Burn Rate for Founders (2026)
https://zensus.finance/blog/runway-vs-burn-rate-for-founders

The difference between runway, burn rate, net burn, gross burn, and burn multiple, the formulas, and the founder decisions they inform. Key facts from the guide:

- Burn rate is the speed at which a startup consumes cash; runway is how long that cash lasts at that speed. Neither tells you when a payment might fail.
- Gross burn = total operating cash outflows. Net burn = operating cash outflows - operating cash inflows. Runway (months) = available cash / average monthly net burn.
- Use cash collected, not revenue: $100,000 of expenses against $45,000 collected is $55,000 of net burn, not $20,000 against $80,000 of booked revenue.
- Example: $1,200,000 with $100,000 of net burn is 12 months; hiring two engineers adds $25,000 a month and cuts runway to 9.6 months.
- Monthly averages hide timing: a company opening June with $100,000 that pays $85,000 of payroll on June 5 and a $25,000 vendor on June 9 goes to -$10,000 on June 9, even though it ends the month at $50,000.
- Carta data: startups that raised a Series A in Q4 2024 had waited a median of 774 days since seed (about 2.1 years), up from 420 days in Q4 2021. Plan runway around milestones and delays rather than a fixed 18 to 24 months.
- Burn multiple compares net burn with net new ARR; lower is better, and around 2x is a commonly cited rule of thumb (David Sacks).
- Track available cash, monthly net burn with a three-month trend, and the first projected cash shortfall (the date cash dips below your floor).

### Default Alive vs Default Dead for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/default-alive-vs-default-dead-for-founders

Whether a startup reaches profitability before its cash runs out, using Paul Graham's 2015 default alive / default dead test, with a founder checklist. Key facts from the guide:

- Default alive: at today's growth and spending, the company reaches profitability before cash runs out, without new money. Default dead: cash runs out first. Both are forecasts, not fate.
- Four inputs: available cash, current monthly revenue (cash collected, not ARR), recent monthly revenue growth, and monthly operating expenses. Growing from $40,000 to $50,000 over four months is about 5.7% compound monthly growth.
- Find two dates: break-even (revenue covers expenses) and the first cash shortfall. If break-even comes first the company is default alive; if cash runs out first it is default dead.
- Worked example: $300,000 of cash, $50,000 of monthly revenue, $90,000 of monthly expenses. At 10% monthly growth revenue passes expenses in month 8 with about $152,000 left (default alive); at 3% cash goes negative in month 9 while break-even is not until month 21 (default dead). Cutting expenses to $70,000 at 3% growth reaches break-even by month 13.
- Runway ($300,000 / $40,000 = 7.5 months) assumes nothing changes; burn multiple (net burn / net new ARR, David Sacks) measures efficiency, not survival.
- Month-end balances hide timing: $20,000 + $60,000 - $50,000 = $30,000 at month-end, but payroll on the 15th before a payment on the 25th takes the balance to -$30,000.
- Graham's "fatal pinch" is default dead + slow growth + not enough time to fix it.
- Zensus projects cash on real dates, shows the month cash is projected to run out, and tests a scenario (hiring, churn, pricing, one-off costs) against the baseline; its runway calculator estimates cash duration and is not a default alive calculator.

### ARR vs Cash for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/arr-vs-cash-for-founders

Why ARR and bank balance diverge for SaaS companies. Key facts from the guide:

- ARR measures recurring revenue sold; cash flow measures money actually in the bank. Companies spend cash, not ARR.
- A $120,000 annual prepaid contract adds $120,000 to cash on day one but only $10,000 of recognized revenue per month.
- Deferred revenue is cash collected before service is delivered; it is not the same as available liquidity.
- Two companies at $1M ARR can have completely different runway depending on annual vs monthly billing mix.
- Subscription cash flow forecasting requires billing schedules, renewal timing, and collections behavior, not ARR alone.
- Zensus syncs HubSpot subscriptions and projects when annual and quarterly contracts hit the bank, not flat monthly spreads.

### Cash Conversion Cycle
https://zensus.finance/blog/cash-conversion-cycle

What the cash conversion cycle (CCC) is, how to calculate it, and how founders use it with a cash flow forecast. Key facts from the guide:

- CCC = Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) − Days Payable Outstanding (DPO).
- A longer CCC generally means more cash is tied up in inventory and receivables before customer collections return it to the bank.
- The same CCC headline can hide different bottlenecks: a 45-day CCC can be an inventory problem or a collections problem depending on DIO vs DSO.
- A negative CCC means customers pay before suppliers must be paid, which can reduce working capital needs when the business model supports it.
- CCC does not replace a cash flow forecast or runway model; payroll, one-time purchases, and fundraising delays can still create a cash shortage.
- Worked example at a $10,000/day sales rate: moving from 30-day to 60-day DSO can create about $300,000 of additional receivables funding need.
- Zensus connects Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot so collections timing, payables, and runway move in one forecast with scenarios and Slack alerts.

### Can QuickBooks Forecast Cash Flow?
https://zensus.finance/blog/can-quickbooks-forecast-cash-flow

Yes, QuickBooks Online can forecast cash flow; the guide covers its features, a step-by-step setup, its limits, and when another tool makes sense. Key facts from the guide:

- Intuit documents a 13-week cash flow forecast grid in QuickBooks Online Simple Start, Essentials, Plus, and Advanced, with beginning cash, money in, money out, and ending cash, plus open invoices, recurring bills, manual projections, and AI predictions.
- Expected dates can be changed or transactions excluded without editing the original invoice or bill; projections can be one-time or repeating and do not change the books.
- The cash runway card estimates how many months cash may last from average spending over the past three months, which is not the same as finding the week cash falls below a threshold.
- Intuit Intelligence adds 12-month forecasts and scenario analysis and needs at least two years of transaction history; Intuit Enterprise Suite adds three-way financial forecasts.
- Worked example: a $60,000 customer payment arriving two weeks late leaves the month-end balance at $85,000 but drops the lowest week from $55,000 to $25,000, $15,000 below a $40,000 reserve.
- QuickBooks Desktop 2022 and later have no Cash Flow Projector. Zensus is independent of Intuit and builds a weekly forecast on QuickBooks Online data, Plaid bank data, and HubSpot invoices and subscriptions.

### Zero Cash Date for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/zero-cash-date-for-founders

How to calculate when your cash runs out from dated receipts and payments instead of a monthly runway average. Key facts from the guide:

- A zero cash date is the first point projected available cash reaches zero; track it alongside the first negative balance and the first cash-floor breach.
- Runway is a duration (available cash divided by average monthly net burn); the zero cash date is a calendar point, found by rolling cash forward week by week.
- $300,000 at $50,000 a month looks like six months, but with $30,000 biweekly payroll, a $36,000 prepayment in week 1, and a $100,000 customer renewal arriving in week 22, cash first goes negative in week 20, about 4.5 months in.
- A positive week-end balance can hide a shortfall: $50,000, then $40,000 payroll on Nov 2, a $25,000 vendor payment on Nov 4 (minus $15,000), and a $35,000 receipt on Nov 6 ends the week at $20,000.
- A $30,000 cash floor is breached on Nov 2, two days before the first negative balance; weekly models show the week at risk, daily schedules show the day.
- Zensus builds a weekly forecast from Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot data, shows the projected cash-out month, and sends Slack alerts on a cash floor.

### Why Your HubSpot Revenue Numbers Don't Tell the Whole Cash Story
https://zensus.finance/blog/hubspot-pipeline-to-cash-forecast

How to forecast cash from HubSpot invoices, subscriptions, and payment records rather than from sales reports. Key facts from the guide:

- HubSpot shows revenue, not cash: its revenue reporting separates pipeline forecasts, booked revenue, billed revenue, and collected revenue, and a payment marked paid in HubSpot is not the same as cash deposited in the bank.
- Start from open invoices, outstanding balances, due dates, and scheduled subscription billing, then estimate when each payment will actually reach the bank.
- HubSpot invoice statuses are Draft, Open, Paid, and Void; a partially paid invoice stays Open, so forecast only the remaining balance ($6,000 left on a $10,000 invoice with $4,000 paid).
- Subscription statuses (Active, Scheduled, Unpaid, Paused, Canceled, Expired) each need different treatment; keep an Unpaid subscription out of the baseline.
- Two companies with $12,000 of MRR can collect cash very differently: $12,000 every month, or $144,000 once a year.
- A payment marked Succeeded in HubSpot is not necessarily in the bank; manually recorded payments are Succeeded when recorded, and processors pay out on their own schedule.
- Worked example from October 27, 2026: $48,000 of expected receipts, only $6,000 before Nov 10 and $42,000 in the week of Nov 10; from $20,000 of starting cash the month ends at $31,000, but even on schedule cash dips to $7,000 on Nov 12, when a $10,000 vendor bill goes out before the larger invoices land.
- When HubSpot, QuickBooks, Stripe, and the bank all hold records of the same transaction, link them so each collection is counted once; HubSpot does not sync a QuickBooks payment applied to several invoices.
- Zensus reads HubSpot invoices and subscriptions (not deals) alongside bank and QuickBooks data, and sends a Slack alert when the 30-day projection drops below a user's floor.

### 27 Pay Periods in 2026 or 2027?
https://zensus.finance/blog/27-pay-periods-2026-2027

Which year has 27 biweekly pay dates, why sources disagree, and what the extra payroll run costs. Key facts from the guide:

- A biweekly payroll has 27 pay dates in a calendar year only when a payday lands on January 1 (or on January 1 or 2 in a leap year). For one schedule that happens about once every 11 years.
- January 1 and December 31, 2027 are both Fridays, so a biweekly schedule with a payday on Friday, January 1, 2027 has 27 pay dates on the 2027 calendar.
- January 1, 2027 is a Federal Reserve holiday and ACH payments do not settle on federal holidays. If that payday is paid early, on Thursday, December 31, 2026, the 27th pay date moves into 2026 and 2027 has 26.
- The federal payroll calendar published by the General Services Administration shows this: 27 pay dates in 2026, ending December 31, and 26 in 2027.
- The 27th run adds 1/26, about 3.8 percent, to payroll cash for the year. At $40,000 a run, the year costs $1,080,000 instead of $1,040,000.
- An annual salary divided by 27 instead of 26 lowers every paycheck. The federal exemption test in 29 CFR 541.600 is per pay period ($684 a week, $1,368 biweekly), so a $36,000 salary clears it at 26 paychecks ($1,384.62) and not at 27 ($1,333.33).
- Annual limits such as the 401(k) deferral limit ($24,500 in 2026, per the IRS) do not grow with an extra payday.

### Cash Flow Forecasting for Agencies
https://zensus.finance/blog/cash-flow-forecasting-for-agencies

A 13-week cash flow guide for agencies: retainers, payroll, and late payments. Key facts from the guide:

- A profitable agency can still run out of cash: the forecast asks what the lowest bank balance will be over the next 13 weeks, and when to act before it.
- Closing cash = opening cash + cash receipts that clear - cash payments that leave, repeated for 13 weeks and compared with a minimum operating cash floor.
- Four timing gaps drive agency cash problems: payment terms (advance vs. arrears billing, milestone splits), late payment, pass-through costs such as media spend paid before the client reimburses, and fixed payroll dates.
- Schedule receipts on the date they clear and payments on their actual debit dates; if net-30 clients consistently pay at day 45, use day 45. Keep unsigned pipeline in an upside scenario, not the baseline.
- Worked example: an agency with $50,000 in cash and a $30,000 floor collects $98,000 and pays $84,000 over five weeks, ending at $64,000, but week 3 closes at $13,000, $17,000 below the floor. Had the second $25,000 retainer arrived in week 3 instead of week 4, week 3 would have been $38,000.
- Stress tests: the biggest client paying 21 days late, a canceled retainer (costs such as payroll, software and rent stay), and fronting a $25,000 media campaign for four weeks.
- Four weekly metrics: client collection time, lowest projected cash balance, payroll coverage, and pass-through exposure.
- Zensus covers QuickBooks invoice inputs, bank-linked payroll, and what-if scenarios, but it does not learn each client's payment habits, so collection assumptions still need review.

### How to Build a 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast in Excel
https://zensus.finance/blog/how-to-build-a-13-week-cash-flow-forecast-in-excel

An eight-step build of a 13-week cash flow forecast in Excel, in the same layout as the free Zensus template. Key facts from the guide:

- The sheet has 13 weekly columns (B to N): dates in row 5, opening cash in row 6, cash in in rows 8 to 10, total cash in in row 11, cash out in rows 13 to 18, total cash out in row 19, net cash flow in row 20, closing balance in row 21, the cash floor in row 23, and the status check in row 24.
- Six formulas do the calculating: total cash in =SUM(B8:B10), total cash out =SUM(B13:B18), net cash flow =B11-B19, closing balance =B6+B20, next opening balance =B21, and the floor check =IF(B21<$B$23,"BELOW FLOOR","OK"). Week dates step with =B5+7.
- Enter each amount in the week the cash moves: a $20,000 invoice sent in week 2 on 30-day terms from a customer who pays 10 days late belongs in week 7. Biweekly payroll goes only in the weeks it is paid, never divided across every week.
- Worked example: $100,000 opening cash and a $25,000 floor, with $12,000 collected every week and $28,000 biweekly payroll plus $6,000 payroll taxes. The quarter ends at $42,500, but week 7 closes at $23,500 and week 11 at $15,500. Moving a $9,000 software renewal a week later and a $48,000 receipt a week earlier clears both.
- A positive week-end balance can hide a mid-week shortfall: $20,000 on Monday and a $30,000 payroll on Tuesday leave the account $10,000 short before a Friday collection.
- Update every Monday: compare last week to the bank, archive it as actuals, roll the weeks forward, and add a new week 13. Four quick tests catch broken links and overwritten formulas.
- Zensus does the same from bank (Plaid), QuickBooks, and HubSpot data, with monthly, weekly, daily, and 13-week views and Slack alerts when the 30-day projection drops below a threshold.

### MCP vs CLI for Finance Teams
https://zensus.finance/blog/mcp-vs-cli-for-finance-teams

A finance team's guide to letting AI touch financial data, comparing Model Context Protocol (MCP) with command-line (CLI) scripts. Key facts from the guide:

- MCP is built for AI to discover and call approved tools in a chat; CLI is for running commands you have already defined, such as a Monday report.
- Neither is inherently more secure. Permissions, audit trails, and keeping AI from making changes have to be designed in either case.
- Microsoft's Dynamics 365 ERP MCP server acts within the authenticated user's security role, and QuickBooks has an MCP connector for Google Gemini.
- The recommended setup is hybrid: AI retrieves data through MCP, a controlled script validates it, a deterministic engine calculates the forecast, and a human approves before anything is posted.
- Zensus is not an MCP server; it reads bank, QuickBooks, and HubSpot data to build a cash forecast and never posts entries or moves money.

## Free Tools

### Zero Cash Date and Startup Runway Calculator
https://zensus.finance/tools/runway-calculator

Free interactive calculator: enter cash, monthly revenue, and monthly expenses to get your runway in months and your projected zero-cash date. Models hiring impact at 1.3x loaded salary cost and the timing of annual contract payments. No signup required.

### 2027 and 2026 Payroll Calendar and Pay Period Calculator
https://zensus.finance/tools/payroll-calendar

Free tool: every 2026 and 2027 pay date for weekly, biweekly, semimonthly and monthly schedules, with period start and end dates, paydays moved off weekends and Federal Reserve holidays to the previous banking day, 26 or 27 pay periods, three-paycheck months, monthly payroll cash impact, and Excel, CSV and ICS downloads. The page also lists the 2027 pay dates for the common schedules in plain text and the 2026 and 2027 Federal Reserve holidays.

### 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast Template and Builder
https://zensus.finance/tools/13-week-cash-flow-template

Free tool: the 13-week cash flow forecast template (XLSX, formulas in place, no email) plus a browser builder for a first 13-week forecast. Inputs: opening balance, cash buffer floor, week 1 start date, customer collections per week, payroll per run and pay frequency (placed on pay dates: weekly, biweekly, semimonthly on the 15th and month end, or monthly at month end), monthly bills (placed in the week that holds the 1st), other weekly spend, and a one-off inflow in a chosen week. Outputs: the lowest balance and its week, the first week that closes below the floor, the week 13 closing balance, a 13-row table, a CSV download in the template's layout, and an optional emailed copy.

## Comparisons

### Zensus vs Float
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-float

Honest comparison for founders evaluating Float alternatives, based on vendor pages as of September 2026. Float: Essentials $130/mo billed monthly ($105/mo annually), Growth $265/mo, Scale $389/mo; Xero and QuickBooks Online; no direct bank connection (bank data arrives through the accounting platform); 13-week rolling view and up to 36-month forecasts on Growth and Scale; unlimited users; multi-entity consolidation on Scale; 14-day trial, no credit card. Zensus: flat $199/mo, Plaid plus QuickBooks plus HubSpot, plain-English scenarios, Slack alerts; 14-day trial with a card collected at signup and not charged until the trial ends.

### Zensus vs Pulse
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-pulse

Honest comparison for Pulse app alternatives, based on vendor pages as of September 2026. Pulse: $29/mo Basics, $59/mo Small Business Plan (adds QuickBooks Online sync), $89/mo Premium (currency conversion), manual scenario toggles, 30-day trial with a card required at signup. Zensus: $199/mo automated forecast from bank and CRM data with subscription-aware timing.

### Zensus vs Cash Flow Frog
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-cash-flow-frog

Comparison based on each vendor's own pages, read on 5 October 2026. Cash Flow Frog: one Pro Plan priced by annual revenue, $69/mo up to $1M, $89/mo to $5M, $129/mo to $10M, $179/mo to $20M and $249/mo above $20M on monthly billing, with lower yearly rates; 14-day trial with no credit card; seven accounting systems (QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Xero, Sage Intacct, Odoo, Zoho Books, FreshBooks), Plaid for US and Canadian banks, Excel or CSV import; forecasts up to 36 months; unlimited entities and native multi-currency; no CRM connection per its own pages, with deals pushed in through Zapier; plain-English scenarios through an external assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini). Zensus: $199/mo flat at any revenue, QuickBooks Online only, direct HubSpot connection for invoices and subscriptions (not deals), a built-in plain-English cash flow agent, Slack alerts on a 30-day projection, one currency per forecast. Cash Flow Frog is cheaper at every revenue tier below $20M.

### Float alternatives
https://zensus.finance/compare/float-alternatives

Five Float alternatives compared from each vendor's own pages as of September 2026, listed by starting price. Pulse: $29/mo, QuickBooks Online sync from $59/mo, 30-day trial that charges the card at the end. Cash Flow Frog: from $33/mo billed yearly (early-bird rate, set by revenue), seven accounting platforms including Xero and QuickBooks Desktop, direct bank feed via Plaid, no CRM connection, 14-day trial with no card. Futrli: $40/mo excl. VAT for 1 to 5 licenses, daily and 3-way forecasting, Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage, 14-day trial with no card. Helm: $50/mo for the first connected business (currency not stated), Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage Accounting, 12-month forecasts, unlimited scenarios. Zensus: $199/mo, Plaid bank feed, QuickBooks, HubSpot subscription sync, Slack alerts, no Xero. Float stays the better fit for Xero users who need multi-entity consolidation, and Float Essentials ($130/mo) costs less than Zensus.

## QuickBooks Online cash flow forecasting software

https://zensus.finance/quickbooks-cash-flow-forecasting

Product page for businesses on QuickBooks Online. What QuickBooks' own cash flow planner does, in Intuit's words (read October 2026): it projects from QuickBooks data and connected bank accounts; its 24-month view shows 14 months into the future; it is not available when Multicurrency is on. Intuit's other forecasting features, also in Intuit's words: Forecasts in QuickBooks Online Advanced are built from the Profit and Loss, cover income, cost of sales and expenses (not cash), run up to three years, and support accrual accounting only; Intuit Intelligence forecasting projects income, expenses and cash flow for the next 12 months, needs at least 2 years of transaction history, and answers what-if questions in chat. None of these is a sales, demand or purchase-cycle forecast, and Zensus does not forecast demand either; it forecasts cash. The page includes a four-week example projection showing where each number comes from (bank balance from Plaid, invoices and bills from QuickBooks on their due dates, payroll from recurring bank debits, a HubSpot renewal on its billing date). What Zensus adds: QuickBooks invoices and bills placed on their due dates (overdue ones moved forward) and synced daily, a direct bank feed through Plaid, HubSpot subscriptions on their billing dates, monthly, weekly, daily and 13-week views, plain-English scenarios, and Slack alerts. Zensus forecasts in one currency and does not convert. $199/mo, 14-day free trial.

## LLM entity page

https://zensus.finance/llm-info

HTML entity summary for AI crawlers: founder, founded 2025-08, US company, $199/mo pricing, integrations, guides, tools, and links to llms.txt.

### 13-Week Cash Flow Template
https://zensus.finance/templates/13-week-cash-flow-template.xlsx

Free XLSX template: 13 weekly columns with inflow and outflow line items, chained opening and closing balances, net cash flow, and a cash buffer floor check. Works in Excel, Google Sheets, and Numbers. No email required. The template page with the browser builder is https://zensus.finance/tools/13-week-cash-flow-template.
